name: Rain
description: Wildfire mission autonomy for firefighting aircraft; autonomous Black Hawk demos with Sikorsky

paragraphs: Rain adapts military and civil autonomous aircraft to perceive, understand, and suppress wildfires. The company says the technology equips fire agencies with a new layer of safety for human-piloted missions and supports command of a network of uncrewed aircraft prepositioned in remote areas. Its wildfire mission autonomy system perceives the fire, reads its behavior, size and direction of spread, and uses that information to design a suppression strategy.

Rain and Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, have demonstrated autonomous wildfire suppression technology in a representative wildfire environment in California. That work included communication interoperability of an autonomous aircraft with a human-piloted helicopter in the same Fire Traffic Area, supervised by an Orange County Fire Authority air tactical group supervisor aircraft. The two companies also said they would explore how Sikorsky's MATRIX autonomy suite operating with Rain's Wildfire Mission Autonomy System can launch uncrewed helicopters to drop water on wildfires within minutes of detection.

Rain announced a partnership with Brothers Air Support, a private Black Hawk firefighting operator, to equip their helicopter with Rain's wildfire perception system. The work goes back to 2019, when Bryan, Ephraim and Max started building the MK1 prototype. That prototype produced a fully autonomous demonstration of a drone system detecting and suppressing a wildfire ignition in approximately 40 acres of forest.

quote.text: Rain’s wildfire intelligence system builds a strategy that considers subsequent responding aircraft, incorporating their resources and arrival times into an optimal suppression strategy.

name: BurnBot
description: Remote-operated prescribed burn machines for fuels reduction without smoke/escape risk

paragraphs: BurnBot sells wildfire fuels management, equipping infrastructure operators, communities, agencies and ecological partners with tools and services. The work runs from fire mitigation and fuels management to timber operations.

The equipment is remote-controlled masticators and blackline machines. Crews pair the machines with real-time telemetry and monitoring. Because operators work remotely, treatments can be made in steep, remote or hazardous areas. The company says the machines run around the clock in most weather conditions. Prescribed burning uses controlled ignition systems on land and in the air. Projects are documented with dynamic treatment maps and fuel load models.

Government customers are described as federal, state, tribal and local land managers. On the community side, the site names WUI neighborhoods, fire safe councils and cooperatives. The company says it is a qualified contractor for both personnel and equipment, supporting state and federal agencies. It says it was built by fire practitioners, scientists and foresters. Its headquarters is in South San Francisco, California.

paragraphs: First Due sells cloud software that fire and EMS agencies use to run records and daily operations in one place. The suite pulls incident reporting, prevention, pre-incident planning, scheduling, assets, hydrants, training and mobile response behind a single login.

Incident documentation is built around the national fire reporting standard, with dynamic forms and error checking at submission. The patient care record is written to the NEMSIS data standard. It reads from cardiac monitors so crews do not key the same values twice. Pre-incident plans hold hazardous materials detail down to chemical location and quantity. Those plans can layer in GIS data through an Esri partnership.

The site describes CAL FIRE moving from a December decision to a July go-live. A county fire department is described using it to coordinate inspections and share preplan information with response crews. The company claims it accounts for nearly half of all NERIS submissions nationwide.

paragraphs: Technosylva sells wildfire and extreme weather risk software to electric utilities and fire agencies. The point of it is turning complicated weather data into something a planning or response team can act on.

For planning, the company combines large numbers of validated fire simulations with historical weather and a customer's own asset data. Its models estimate what an ignition would mean in acres burned, buildings destroyed and people affected. For operations, simulations run nightly to produce the wildfire risk metrics crews plan around. Utilities use the output to target power shutoffs instead of cutting service broadly. Feeds from computer-aided dispatch and IRWIN bring in incidents from federal and state agencies. Flooding, high wind, extreme temperature and winter storms sit in the same view as fire.
The homepage points readers toward Xcel Energy, CAL FIRE and CORE. Bryan Spear is named as chief executive. The company has also announced modeling of urban conflagration in the built environment.

name: Dryad Networks
description: Solar-powered gas sensors under the forest canopy for ultra-early fire detection

paragraphs: Dryad provides ultra-early wildfire detection and autonomous drone systems for public and private forests. The sensors are meant to detect fires within minutes from ignition so firefighters can put them out before they spread out of control.

The fourth generation sensor combines VOC, CO and PM2.5 sensing to catch a fire as early as the smoldering phase. The units form a wireless environmental sensor network based on LoRaWAN. A patented distributed architecture is meant to allow large-scale deployments in areas without existing network coverage. A cloud platform handles deployment planning, operation, analytics and alerting for those networks. An observation drone is dispatched when a sensor detects a fire, and a second drone applies fire suppressant liquids to extinguish fires autonomously.

Beyond forest owners, the company pitches utility and grid operators on protection against liabilities. Published case studies include a fire in Lebanon stopped by early detection. The founders say they came to this work after several startups and exits in IT, electronics and telecommunications.

name: Frontline Wildfire Defense
description: Exterior retardant/foam systems and app-based wildfire defense for homes and HOAs

paragraphs: Frontline Wildfire Defense sells exterior sprinkler systems and companion software that defend homes and businesses against wildfire. The company describes its mission as providing faster, safer and more precise ways to protect homes, families, businesses and communities from wildfire.

The second-generation defense system is tied to fire tracking software and turns on automatically when fire comes within seven miles of a home. Once running, it saturates the property with water and biodegradable firefighting foam to create conditions the company calls too wet to burn. A commercial version is aimed at businesses, campuses and critical infrastructure, meant to cut risk before a fire reaches the property. A companion app carries wildfire alerts, maps, fire danger indexes, emergency contact groups and evacuation checklists.

Homeowners, businesses and new housing developments are the audience, and the company says its system will safeguard 151 homes at a Woodside Homes community. Installation is handled by licensed contractors in each state rather than by the company itself. Financing options, including zero-down wildfire protection, are offered to buyers. The company points to embers as the central danger, saying they cause up to 90% of structure loss during a wildfire.

paragraphs: Perimeter sells a public safety platform that pairs evacuation planning with situational awareness mapping, delivered through Perimeter Plan and Perimeter Map. Perimeter Plan is used before an incident to set safe points, evacuation routes, and critical infrastructure points. During an incident, hazards, road closures, and evacuation orders are published to a map that updates for every agency and the public.

The platform is aimed at emergency managers, public information officers, law enforcement agencies, and fire departments. The public facing map is shareable to anyone needing emergency information, with no download or sign up required. Agencies can grant access to neighboring jurisdictions and mutual aid partners.

Data created in Perimeter is stored for after action analysis. Saved detail is meant to be ready to share when records are requested by stakeholders. Perimeter exports KML and GeoJSON and integrates Esri data with existing tools.

paragraphs: Flock Safety sells license plate readers, video cameras, gunshot detection and response drones to law enforcement agencies, schools, businesses and neighborhoods to help them deter crime, respond to emergencies and investigate safety incidents. Its license plate recognition cameras capture plates and vehicle characteristics such as make, color and body type to generate investigative leads. Responders get an instant alert when a vehicle matches a customer-defined or NCIC hot list. Users include law enforcement agencies, businesses, neighborhoods, apartment complexes, houses of worship and schools.

Beyond plate readers, Flock sells PTZ video cameras for open areas such as parking lots, intersections and parks, and fixed cameras for buildings and city streets. A gunshot and audio detection product verifies gunfire and links each alert with nearby LPR reads and video. Flock DFR, its drone as first responder system, launches a docked drone to the coordinates of a 911 call, LPR hit or gunshot alert and streams live video to officers before they arrive. Solar-powered mobile trailers cover parking lots, retail centers and construction sites, and an optional Alert Response Service puts trained agents on live alerts.

Flock sells on an annual subscription that covers hardware, software, maintenance and support. The company has reduced its recommended default data retention from 30 days to 7 days, which it says applies to new law enforcement customers. Customers control their data and how it is shared, and every search is logged.

paragraphs: Skydio makes autonomous drones, along with the docks and software to run them, and sells drone programs to customers from energy networks to neighborhood precincts to battlefields. Those programs cover Drone as First Responder, automated inspection and site security. Dock for X10 positions Skydio X10 drones at a site so that missions launch remotely without anyone present. The smaller Skydio R10 puts eyes indoors before officers enter.

Skydio states that more than 1,500 public safety agencies use its drones. In a Drone as First Responder program, Skydio says its drones launch in under 20 seconds and reach incidents autonomously in under 90 seconds. DFR Command is the software from which remote operators launch and manage drones, respond to multiple calls and stream live video to patrol and command. It integrates with RapidSOS and CAD at dispatch, Axon Fusus for live operations, and automatic evidence upload into Axon Evidence. Skydio's customer stories include Brookhaven PD, which it says reached 30 second response times after deploying 8 Docks.

Skydio Site Security uses the same dock-based drones to verify alarms, patrol perimeters and deliver live visibility across a site. paragraphs: SoundThinking, Inc., listed on Nasdaq as SSTI, sells AI and data-driven public safety technology to law enforcement, civic leadership, and security professionals. Its ShotSpotter system detects and verifies gunfire incidents in near real time to support awareness and response. ShotSpotter is one part of the SafetySmart Platform, which the company says unifies gunfire alerts, vehicle intelligence, investigations, field awareness, and operational context in one place.

Alongside ShotSpotter, the platform includes CrimeTracer, a law enforcement search engine, and CaseBuilder, an investigation management system. ResourceRouter directs patrol and community anti-violence resources to where they will have the most effect. SafePointe screens entry points in high-traffic environments for weapons. PlateRanger connects vehicle sightings across time, location, and related events for investigators.

The company was founded as ShotSpotter in 1996 by physicist Dr. Robert Showen, who was then locating earthquake epicenters at the Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California. After hearing gunshots in a nearby neighborhood, he applied the sound wave principles from his earthquake research to detecting and locating gunfire. Ralph Clark, hired as CEO in 2010, moved the system to a subscription rather than a capital hardware purchase. He also brought the human review of potential gunshots in-house through a centralized Incident Review Center. The gunshot detection service now serves over 170 cities. In 2023 the company rebranded from ShotSpotter to SoundThinking and launched the SafetySmart Platform. It reports more than 300 customers and work with approximately 2,100 agencies.

brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

profile_research.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

paragraphs: City Detect sells a camera and software service that helps municipalities and counties find and address urban blight before complaints pile up. Cameras ride on a city's existing fleet vehicles and collect images of properties as those vehicles drive their normal routes. The company's PASS AI then detects and maps signs of urban blight and decay from the public right of way.

Roof-mounted data collection units capture street-level imagery during routine city operations. paragraphs: CENTEGIX sells emergency alerting for schools, built around a solution called CrisisAlert that lets any staff member call for help. The alert carries the exact floor, room or hallway rather than just a building name.

When a full alert fires, strobes and intercoms activate across the campus. Arriving responders are shown the precise location of the person who pressed the button. The company is careful to say that most of what it handles is not an active shooter but a medical emergency, a behavioral crisis or a student leaving campus. Around the alerting sit other modules, including visitor management for authenticating and locating people on campus. Reunification is handled the same way, with a guardian verified before any student is handed over. Rollout starts with a short discovery call that maps buildings and looks for gaps in response.

School districts are the core audience, with the product framed as giving staff the confidence to act quickly. The same technology is offered to healthcare organizations facing workplace violence. A third line is aimed at public servants and the staff who work alongside them. The company says the product was built by former educators, law enforcement officers and caregivers. It also convenes an invitation-only customer advisory board drawn from senior safety leaders.

paragraphs: EffiGov builds AI phone agents for local government. Every department gets its own agent, trained on that department's own services, hours, and escalation rules. The buyers are cities, counties, and special districts.

paragraphs: Bamboo Health sells software that joins behavioral and physical health data into a longitudinal patient record and places it inside the systems clinicians already work in. Its audiences include community and behavioral health providers and federally qualified health centers. Accountable care organizations and other provider groups are addressed separately.

Alerts are driven by admission, discharge and transfer feeds, and care navigation can be started from inside an electronic health record. For people with substance use disorder, prescription drug monitoring program data and alerts are used to flag risk and guide patients toward care. Care navigators also review rosters by hand to find high utilizers whose behavioral health needs have gone unmet. Behavioral health referrals and crisis resource availability sit alongside that history in one place.

The company took its present form in 2021, when Appriss Health acquired PatientPing and rebranded. It claims a footprint across 52 states and territories. Encounters on its network are put at 3 billion a year. Published material points to work with the State of Delaware on crisis care and behavioral health coordination.

paragraphs: Unite Us sells software and data infrastructure for coordinating whole-person care across healthcare, government and community-based organizations. Its named audiences include public health and human services agencies. Managed care and Medicaid plans are also on that list.

The core product is a closed-loop referral system for sending and receiving electronic social care referrals within a network of community partners. Staff can run social needs screenings, after which the platform automatically suggests resources or referrals. A secure chat feature lets users at partner organizations message each other about shared referrals, cases and clients. Alongside referrals, the company sells predictive analytics meant to predict long-term risks and measure impact. Its Population Insights tool combines social, economic, environmental and health information with modeling to identify at-risk populations. It also automates payments to community-based organizations. The company states that it partnered with Presbyterian Health Plan to create New Mexico's first statewide closed-loop referral system.

paragraphs: ES&S has supplied election systems since 1979, describing them as secure, accessible and accurate. By its own account the systems are paper based, certified and fully auditable. They are sold to jurisdictions large and small.

The ExpressVote XL displays the full ballot on a 32-inch interactive screen and produces an independent voter-verifiable paper record. name: Hart InterCivic
description: Verity voting systems: tabulation, ballot marking, and election management for counties

paragraphs: Hart InterCivic sells voting systems and election services to the officials who run elections. In one configuration, voters mark a paper ballot with a pen and the ballot is scanned to capture the vote digitally. A hybrid option combines touchscreen voting with a voter-verifiable paper trail. Absentee and mail ballots are handled through central scanning.

On the paper-based products, voter choices are never encoded in a digital seal for tabulation. Products carry role-based controls meant to keep an election transparent end to end. The company announced certification of a newer product line, Vanguard, to the VVSG 2.0 standard by the Election Assistance Commission. Within that line, Flex is a universal ballot marking device. Vault handles the scanning of ballots, whether marked by hand or by machine. Workspace covers end-to-end election management.

Hart says it has worked side by side with election professionals for more than 100 years. Its regional offices span coast to coast. The company also states that Vanguard is the only voting system available in the United States that delivers on both the latest EAC standard and the conditions of the executive order it cites.

name: JusticeText
description: AI evidence transcription and analysis (bodycam, interrogation) for public defenders and DAs

paragraphs: JusticeText sells evidence review software for criminal defense work, turning hours of audio and video discovery into searchable transcripts synced to the original media. The platform transcribes and translates media in more than 100 languages, including files where several languages are spoken. An assistant called MirandaAI works across every piece of evidence in a case to uncover connections. Attorneys can build case timelines, spot inconsistencies and flag key moments across the evidence.

Video clipping, redaction and closed captioning tools are offered for building court exhibits. Multiple camera angles can be synced into one timeline aligned by date and time of capture. Uploaded content is stored on encrypted servers in the United States, encrypted in transit and at rest. The product page states that evidence is never used to train third-party machine learning models. Account access is protected with multi-factor authentication and single sign-on support.

The buyers named on these pages are criminal defense teams, described as thousands of attorneys across the United States. The Kentucky Department of Public Advocacy brought on JusticeText in 2023 for digital evidence review. Harris County Public Defenders are described as drawing insights from large quantities of audiovisual evidence with it. Private defense practices appear as well, including Rossen Law Firm, whose founder uses it to review evidence and create exhibits for court.

name: i-Probe
description: Connected-vehicle road condition monitoring and pavement analytics for DOTs and counties (SoftBank-backed JV)

paragraphs: i-Probe monitors road conditions with connected vehicles, which the pages define as vehicles that use bidirectional communications to address road conditions, safety, system efficiency, or mobility on roadways. The pages address road management agencies and describe the offering as more economical, rapid, and consistent road condition monitoring. The technology leverages factory-installed sensors already built into later-model production vehicles, developed in partnership with Honda Motors, and requires no aftermarket equipment.

Connected vehicles collect road roughness data either through crowdsourcing or through a single-vehicle service. That roughness data is processed under an i-Probe algorithm to identify pavement distresses and severity, and the outputs are mapped and tabulated in a cloud dashboard. Distress identification and classification are automated and paired with video verification. Reasons given for choosing the service include results correlated to IRI. Wide-area monitoring of an entire road network is listed among those reasons.
The page names county and municipal public works agencies as one group served. Pavement maintenance service providers are named as the other group served.

On the delivery side it coordinates contracts, schedules, costs and field work so teams can hold to the original plan and keep a complete audit trail. Agencies can change forms, workflows, business rules and dashboards through configuration rather than code. Routing is handled by a separate optimization tool for building efficient multi-stop routes.

Government and public sector fleets are one of the segments the company addresses. For those buyers it points to real-time GPS built for emergency operations. paragraphs: Azuga sells GPS fleet tracking and dual-facing dashcam software meant to keep vehicles, assets and drivers safe. The company argues that such software should improve safety and not only day-to-day operations. It pitches the product as simple to use, affordable, customizable, and easy to install.

The company frames the work as a four-part improvement process folded into daily fleet operations. Driver scoring is meant to show managers and drivers alike how safely they are driving. A mobile app included in the subscription gives administrators and drivers separate views. For tools and small equipment, Bluetooth beacons are picked up by the company's cellular asset trackers. One tracker can detect and report on fifty beacons at a time. Vehicles that leave the factory with built-in telematics can connect to the platform without aftermarket hardware.

Azuga says customers have relied on it since 2013 for GPS fleet tracking and asset tracking. Insurance companies use its telematics data to measure and price risk in commercial vehicle portfolios. The company also says it works with government agencies on how transportation taxes, emissions data and tolls are collected. States and municipalities, it states, use the data to understand traffic patterns and road surface conditions.

Work templates can be defined by each agency so that task structures, fields, and workflows match its own operational processes. Forms built inside the platform can include required fields, dropdowns, conditional logic, and photo or video uploads. The company began as an internal startup within SADA Systems Inc. The full team and product suite divested in early 2023 to form AtomAI Solutions, Inc. as an independent company. name: Blyncsy
description: AI detection of pavement markings and road defects from crowdsourced dashcams (Bentley Systems)

paragraphs: Blyncsy helps cities and state departments of transportation automate their roadway maintenance and asset inventory activities. Rather than sending crews out to look, it works from crowd-sourced dash camera imagery.

Machine learning algorithms and image processing applied to that imagery detect where and when pavement needs maintenance. Condition assessments run from pot holes to paint striping and crosswalk conditions. Paint lines are rated from 1, the worst, to 5, the best. In construction zones the same imagery detects work zone equipment to put those zones on the map. Those detections can also check whether a maintenance of traffic plan matches reality. A further model detects the presence of debris on and beside the road. The AI also estimates the size of the debris it finds.

Results are delivered directly into OpenGIS or another preferred platform. The company claims savings of up to 90% compared to traditional manual inspections. It puts the cost at $10 per centerline mile against $200 or more for a LiDAR scan. News items on the site include a City of Fort Worth partnership on the first phase of automated asset inventory. Another announces a sustainability partner designation in the Google Cloud Partner Advantage Program.

paragraphs: GeoCivix sells cloud-based software that cities, counties and municipalities use to run permitting, licensing, inspections, plan review and citizen services from one system. The pitch is a replacement for paper-based workflows with digital applications, automated routing, electronic plan review, mobile inspections and online payments.

paragraphs: Chorus Intelligence sells the Chorus Intelligence Suite, software that investigators use to manage every stage of a digital investigation from one dashboard. The customers page says it is used every day to help combat serious and organised crime, fraud, human trafficking and terrorism.

An investigator starts by dragging in raw digital data such as call data records, handset downloads and ANPR, which the suite cleanses and formats automatically. Case studies on the site describe North Wales Police using the data cleansing and analysis tools to find and convict a crossbow murderer. Another describes West Midlands Police using Chorus on what the company calls the largest modern slavery investigation ever conducted in the UK. paragraphs: FaceTec sells face verification software that organizations use to confirm a remote user is real and physically present, both at account onboarding and on later logins. Its products cover 3D liveness checks, KYC and 3D face verification, running from an ordinary 2D camera rather than infrared hardware. During onboarding the software records a quick video selfie, verifies 3D liveness, matches the resulting 3D FaceMap to the photo on the ID and checks the ID for signs of tampering. When the user returns, a new video selfie is compared with the stored FaceMap, and a high match, which FaceTec rates at 1/125M FAR, can grant account access.

FaceTec has run a Spoof Bounty Program since October 2019 and says it has passed Ingenium, Bixelab, Praetorian and iBeta Testing Lab Level 1-5 PAD and IAD testing with 0% FAR. The bounty currently stands at $600,000. The company's stated best practice is for customers to keep users' biometric data, as 3D FaceMap or 3D FaceVector records, on their own servers, which run FaceTec's software inside the customer's firewall.

A related product, UR Codes, carries digitally signed biometric data so a codeholder can prove legal identity and age both in person and remotely. FaceTec says it trained its 3D algorithms with the help of over half a million volunteer testers from over 180 countries. It lists more than 90 channel partners worldwide.

Operators can also use it to remotely investigate, assess and de-escalate tense or hazardous situations, reducing the risk to personnel. paragraphs: Robin Radar Systems makes 360 degree, 3D radar systems that detect, track and classify small flying objects such as birds, bats and drones. It sells them to aviation, defence, security and ecology teams that want a full view of their airspace. Its two main products are IRIS, a 3D drone radar in a 29 kg package, and MAX, a 3D bird detection radar.

IRIS uses micro-doppler classification and deep neural network technology to distinguish blades and rotating parts. It combines 360 degree views, 60 degree elevation and a 5 km instrumented range. A software-only update, Long-Range Mode, lets operators switch between 5 km and 12 km instrumented ranges in minutes. MAX pairs with two software interfaces, Bird Viewer for live airspace and Report Viewer for historical analysis. Airports, airfields and wind farms use the bird and bat radars to react to hazards as they emerge.

The name comes from a 1980 project by the Dutch research institute TNO to prevent bird strikes on Royal Netherlands Air Force planes. Siete Hamminga, now CEO, spun the technology out of TNO in 2010 to found the company. It reports more than 300 radars deployed worldwide and a staff of 150 or more people. In 2024 its shareholders reached an acquisition agreement with the Dutch investment company Parcom. Scarecrow, a maker of bird dispersal and data logging systems based on bio-acoustic technology, is a Robin company.

paragraphs: Lexipol sells policy manuals, training, wellness resources, performance reporting, and grant support to public safety agencies, delivered through one system. Its buyers are the people running those agencies, from fire and police chiefs to risk managers, dispatch supervisors, and city administrators. An agency can begin with a single product, such as Policy or Wellness, and add others as it goes.

The policy product is the core: state-specific manuals researched and written by policy and legal professionals, then kept current as laws and standards change. Personnel acknowledge each policy electronically, which creates an audit trail for accreditation, audits, or legal reviews. paragraphs: AlliConnect sells wellness software to public safety agencies that runs peer support teams, check-ins, referrals and clinical connection in one confidential system of record. Its therapist network is pitched as something other than a directory: therapists who understand the work, matched to the person on a guaranteed timeline. That timeline is scheduling within 24 hours and a first appointment within one week. The site puts the vetted clinician network at over 1,200.

Dashboards connect to a department's CAD and RMS, so critical incident types and cumulative exposure trigger workflows automatically and the data comes back anonymized for reporting. Brief, confidential check-ins cover six domains of wellness, and any risk they identify is routed to the wellness team rather than to command. A custom resource center holds the department's own programs, contacts and links rather than a generic wellness library.

paragraphs: Acusensus sells automated traffic enforcement systems to the road authorities and police agencies that are trying to cut deaths and injuries on the road network. The vendor side is a cloud-based platform covering DBE, MBE, WBE and SBE compliance initiatives. Certification work runs from online applications through agency review to approval. For contract compliance, prime and subcontractor payments are collected, and subcontractors confirm payment directly, monthly or quarterly. Reporting draws on more than 400 standard system reports. A payroll line covers Davis-Bacon and Related Acts, the Service Contract Act, state prevailing wage laws and local living wage ordinances. Grant work runs through BlackCat, from applications to asset management and spend-down tracking.

The company says the software has been implemented at over 400 organizations. It claims one million users regularly access the system to register, prequalify, submit reports, manage grants and review bid solicitations. The site cites over 25 years of vendor program compliance experience. B2Gnow and eComply have joined together into one platform spanning vendor management and labor compliance. Hosting is described as fully redundant, with guaranteed availability of 99.9% and SOC 2 Type 2 certification.

Its about page introduces a leadership team including a co-founder whose patent work in data management led to the founding of the company.

Its touchscreen system brings door control, CCTV, intercoms and paging, access control, and utility monitoring together as one console. The design is open architecture, using commercially available components. A licensed mobile device provides physical security management such as locking control and intercom call-ins. Facilities can install NFC tags for officers to scan while walking watch tours. A wellbeing application monitors detainees in detox, with chronic conditions, or on suicide watch. It uses wrist-worn sensors that track heart rate, skin temperature and blood oxygen saturation and detect tampering.

The jail management platform is browser-based and built for county and local jails, handling inmate records, biometrics and analytical reporting. Those jails, the company writes, face a concentration of acute risks including early-phase medical crises, suicide and violence. Record keeping is described as CJIS-compliant data collection and record management.

Another is a digital ecosystem for incarcerated individuals and their families, with community tools, financial services, and purposeful engagement. A third is an invite-only community where corrections professionals share ideas and gather intelligence. These sit on the company's own platform, the foundation of what it calls its suite of CID solutions.

Encartele was founded in 2004 through the merger of call center technology and inmate communications systems. It has been headquartered in Omaha, Nebraska, ever since. The site credits business owner Scott Moreland with directing the company as the corrections industry changed. Encartele also runs an annual training and networking event for corrections professionals.

paragraphs: Guard1 sells hardware and software that prove where staff have been and when, working with correctional agencies, behavioral healthcare facilities and security teams. The central device is The PIPE, a wand that staff touch to a metal memory button on the wall to document that rounds were completed.

In practice an officer touches the button with the wand, and a red light flash or a beep confirms the check was recorded. A mobile option swaps the wand for a handheld digital logbook that shows a real-time task list of the checks and activities still to be completed. A separate duress system puts a device on staff and visitors that sends a signal once per second. When the button is pressed, the location is shown on a control room monitor.

The company says hundreds of agencies have used The PIPE to document officer rounds and hold defensible logs for inspections and incidents. It puts its corrections figure at over 1400 customers served, including 20+ DOCs, hundreds of county jails, ICE facilities and juvenile facilities. For guard tour work more broadly it dates the product to 1990 and claims over 100,000 customers.

paragraphs: 4Sight Labs sells a biometric monitoring system for correctional facilities, meant to help staff watch over the health of people held in custody. Its main product, OverWatch, is presented as the core of a unified correctional biometric platform built for settings where ordinary monitoring falls short.

People in custody wear sensors that track heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature and motion, along with other indicators of physiological distress. Readings are processed as they arrive, so that anomalies produce structured notifications instead of an after-the-fact review. Thresholds can be set by the facility so staff hear about a pattern that points toward a crisis.

The company says the platform is built for county detention centers, state systems, private facilities and complex housing units. It also states that the technology is designed and manufactured in the United States, with a controlled hardware and firmware supply chain. The site reports that the Harford County Sheriff's Office publicly announced putting OverWatch into its custody and safety strategy.

paragraphs: Cell-Guardian sells a monitoring system that watches people held in cells without physical contact or wearable devices. The buyers are correctional facilities, which the company describes as pressed by inmate welfare, liability, and staff safety demands. The record keeping is presented as protection in itself, in the form of time-stamped, auditable records covering staff and the facility.

The sensor fuses radar, thermal imaging, and computer vision to read temperature, register movement, and flag falls as they happen. Video is recorded, timestamped, and stored in the cloud. The unit itself is water-resistant and tamper-resistant, rated IP41, and mounts on a wall or ceiling. Staff reach it through a secure browser without installing extra software, and it runs over Power-over-Ethernet.

The company names suicide watch units, medical cells, and high-risk housing as the places the system goes in. Cell-Guardian was developed by Rahm Sensor Development, Inc., the team behind the VetGuardian platform. Its company page lists an address in Orlando, Florida.

paragraphs: ECINS sells a license-free cloud system for collaborative case management, built for agencies that coordinate support for vulnerable people. Its case management module is used by tens of thousands of users in the UK, including police, health and councils. The central idea is a single shared record, so a client does not repeat the same information to every agency involved. The company reports results across the UK, the United States and Australia.

Work usually begins in the referral module, which replaces paper forms with secure online forms that clients and practitioners fill in themselves. Once a referral is approved, its information can be transferred into the case management module. Within case management, staff receive alerts for significant activity such as child protection interventions. They can also track commonalities between individuals through search fields such as addresses, vehicle license plates and educational institutions. A client engagement module and a MyPortal app let clients receive reminders, respond to messages and tasks, and ask questions from their phones.

Beyond casework, a community collaboration module lets residents, neighbourhood watch groups, business communities, police and local authorities work together on detailed neighbourhood profiles. A staff tasking and oversight module is described as still in development. The homepage claims thousands of users across multiple countries. The system is sold license-free to encourage wide participation at no extra cost.

paragraphs: Safience sells identity intelligence software that looks only for predefined threats, persons of interest and missing persons, matched against a database built from law enforcement records. The site belongs to Biometrica Systems, Inc., a software and data company that supports federal, state, tribal and local law enforcement and private sector safety teams. Its RTIS and RVIS edge sensors capture a single still image rather than video or audio, and any image that does not match a predefined profile is purged immediately. The company states that an alert follows within 60 seconds of a detection and that database queries return in under 5 seconds.

The database behind the system holds 57.3M+ unique individuals and receives over 50,000 new records per day. Those records come from published law enforcement records, agency JMS/RMS integrations, an OffenderWatch partnership and missing-person records, with no OSINT, social media or consumer data. It also markets the system to airports and mass transit, banks, schools and universities, hospitals, hotels, retailers and stadiums.

A second product, eMotive, turns a one-time criminal background check into a continuous, FCRA-compliant alert system for employers, with written consent required from each monitored individual. Matching for eMotive is performed by a third-party, NIST-approved provider in an isolated environment, and Biometrica staff do not see employee match notifications. Biometrica holds the U.S. patent for System and Method for Continuous Biometric Monitoring.

paragraphs: SurePassID sells deploy-anywhere multi-factor authentication for IT/OT and critical infrastructure, deployable in the cloud, on-premise, or within air-gapped networks. It covers Windows, MacOS, and Linux logins with offline 2FA and fronts cloud and on-prem apps through SAML2, OIDC, and LDAP identity providers. The company cites 99.999% availability, redundancy, and automatic failover, and markets the product for compliance with OMB M-22-09, CMMC 2.0, and NIS2. It supports phishing-resistant MFA through FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys and security keys as well as OATH HOTP, TOTP, and OCRA tokens and mobile push.

SurePassID has provided on-premise MFA since its founding in 2012 and says 50% of its customer base, including Fortune 500 companies, uses it on-premise. It also serves financial services, having introduced a private cloud authentication server for online payments licensed by Visa, MasterCard, American Express, First Data, and Discover. About 33% of its install base runs in air-gapped environments, and it provides air-gapped MFA to 11 of 16 critical infrastructure sectors. It offers turnkey MFA for SCIFs and SAPFs and pre-built integrations for SCADA systems such as EcoStruxure Geo SCADA Expert.

Private cloud deployments run in Microsoft Azure Commercial, GCC, and GCC High and in Amazon AWS and AWS GovCloud. As a SAML 2.0 identity provider it adds MFA to existing IAM tools such as Microsoft Entra, Okta, or Ping, and integrates with Workday, Oracle, and SAP directories.

paragraphs: D-Fend Solutions sells counter-drone systems to military, law enforcement and homeland security agencies. The company describes the approach as non-kinetic and AI-enhanced, built for sensitive and challenging environments.

EnforceAir can operate autonomously or under manual control, and it detects, locates and identifies rogue drones in a protected airspace before taking them over. It is sold in several deployment packages, including a Homeland Security & Law Enforcement Bundle and two tactical configurations, EnforceAir PLUS and EnforceAir2. EnforceAir PLUS, launched in August 2025, adds radar and a jammer to the RF-cyber layer. Beyond agencies, the company says the system has been chosen for large-scale events at stadiums, arenas and open-air venues and for VIP protection.

In an August 2026 press release the company says EnforceAir provided counter-drone security across World Cup host cities and was adopted by more than 20 public safety agencies. Chairman and CEO Zohar Halachmi co-founded the company after founding two mobile and enterprise application start-ups. Its U.S. arm, D-Fend Solutions AD, Inc., is located in McLean, Virginia. In June 2026 the company announced an agreement to be acquired by Motorola Solutions. Its newsroom now states that it has officially joined Motorola Solutions.

paragraphs: Sentrycs makes counter-drone systems that detect, track, identify and mitigate unauthorized drones for defense, homeland security and critical infrastructure environments. Rather than radar, it uses passive RF cyber technology to pick up drone communication signals and locate both the drone and its operator. Detection reports the drone type, serial number and operator position. Mitigation does not jam the drone; the system takes control of it through a cyber takeover. If required, it integrates with other types of effector, including jammers.

The company says a team of communications and radio frequency experts embarked in 2017 on developing modular solutions that could be tailored to each customer's drone environment. The system is built for complex and urban environments, where it aims to minimize interference with surrounding communications. It says its customers include governments, security forces and critical infrastructure operators worldwide. Its blog is aimed partly at law enforcement, with posts on how to legally take down a rogue drone and on lessons from recent UAS attacks.

On November 18th, 2025, Ondas Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) announced it had completed the acquisition of Sentrycs. The announcement describes the company as Sentry CS Ltd., based in Israel. It puts Sentrycs at approximately 200 deployments across six continents in more than 25 countries.

paragraphs: Gatekeeper Systems sells video recording and data systems for transportation, meant to make travel safer for children, passengers, and public safety personnel across several modes. The company says it uses AI, video analytics, thermal cameras, and mobile data collectors to inter-connect public transit assets within intelligent transportation systems.

Its mobile data collectors gather video and audio along with GPS tracking and door open and close events, analyzing the data on the bus itself. Those units are ruggedized and crashworthy, serving as black boxes that hold data for accident investigations. Recorders take analog and IP channels at up to 1080P and 30 frames per second, with independently selectable resolutions. Drive caddies have passed MIL SPEC 810F for shock and vibration, and a thermal system warms the hard drive to its prescribed operating temperature before writing or reading in cold weather.

Fleet software called G4 Vision centralizes system health checks, driver behavior analysis, video management, live streaming, GPS, routing and mapping, and student tracking. An Automated Lane Enforcement product for transit buses is named on the home page. The company describes a Platform-as-a-Service business model. name: Axon Vibe
description: Mobility behavior platform powering operator apps: journey detection, BIBO ticketing (built the MTA app)

paragraphs: Axon Vibe sells a smartphone-based, multi-modal mobility platform to public transport operators and authorities. The idea is to match a rider's predicted travel patterns against real-time traffic on roads and rail, then offer more efficient and less polluting travel options.

Patented location tracking predicts what people are going to do next, and psychological communication interventions are used to shift their behaviour. Riders who respond are rewarded with travel fare incentives financed by green governmental funds, plus rewards provided by local merchants. The platform is also sold to enable automatic ticketing, incentivise behaviour change and optimise customer flow management. For cities, understanding why and how people travel in real time is presented as the basis for more accurate planning.

Door-to-door journey detection powers Deutsche Bahn check-in and be-out ticketing, for example in Greater Nuremberg. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority launched its official MTA app in March 2024. Founded in 2014, the company describes a team of more than 100 software engineers, data scientists, location analytics experts, psychologists and communication specialists. Its predecessor Endoxon delivered core technology for Google Maps and was acquired by Google in 2006.

paragraphs: May Mobility develops autonomous driving technology and brings it to ride-hail platforms, cities, campuses and businesses. Its operations run from rural Minnesota to Atlanta and the dense streets of Japan.

The cornerstone of the technology is a system the company calls Multi-Policy Decision Making. It is described as a real-time, reinforcement-learning AI algorithm. name: Longeye
description: AI investigations platform for law enforcement - exhibited at IACP 2026

competitors.why: AI investigative intelligence over case evidence and jail calls with CJIS-compliant AI chat, sold to the same detective bureau.
AI fusing video, phone extractions and jail calls into case timelines for the same investigator buyer weighing an AI investigations tool.

paragraphs: Longeye sells an AI-powered investigative workspace that law enforcement agencies use to analyze digital evidence. An investigator uploads video, audio, phone extractions, social media exports, financial records, and images, then asks questions in plain language. Every answer links back to the exact moment in a video, recording, message, or image, so a finding can be checked later.

Audio and video are transcribed and translated, with searchable transcripts across Spanish, Mandarin, and 99+ more. Each call then lands on a timeline color-coded by relevancy so the conversations most likely to matter come first. A map view plots GPS tracker pings, Cellebrite extraction data, CDR lat/long, and ALPR hits, with a slider that animates movement over time. A standalone product, Longeye Monitor, applies the same engine to jail call review for corrections agencies and jail facilities.

Longeye says it is deployed across the country, from major metropolitan departments and state bureaus of investigation to corrections intelligence units running jail call analysis. Chief Darrell Lowe of the Redmond Police Department is quoted crediting it with closing gaps in a cold-case homicide. On security, the company states it is SOC 2 Type II certified, isolates evidence per agency on dedicated US infrastructure, and never uses evidence to train a large language model. Longeye has raised $5M in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz's American Dynamism Fund.

quote.text: The truth is buried in the evidence. Longeye finds it 100x faster.

provenance.quote: Longeye is an AI-powered investigative workspace that helps law enforcement agencies analyze digital evidence 100x faster.

paragraphs: Pimloc sells Secure Redact, an automated system for the bulk redaction of personal data from video. It is aimed at private and public organizations that want to automate data privacy compliance while still getting operational value from their video. Customers use it to process video for data subject access requests and freedom of information requests.

The system's models recognize identifiers such as faces, heads and license plates the way a human observer would, then redact and classify them automatically. It can be applied selectively, removing some or all faces or all vehicle registration details, and it is trained to perform on low-definition CCTV footage. Pimloc states that Secure Redact detects and anonymizes over 99% of identifiable PII in security video. It also says redaction with its AI runs 200 times faster than doing the job by hand.

The company says its capabilities are deployed across transport, public safety, telehealth, insurance, retail, policing and local government. A second product, Pholio, classifies visual content, and Pimloc has used it to evaluate automated detection of online harms. Founders Simon Randall, the CEO, and James Leigh, the CTO, co-created the Autographer wearable image capture device at a previous business, and the privacy challenges of always-on capture led them to start Pimloc.

quote.text: Automated anonymization is the only way to keep up with changing privacy legislation and to responsibly unlock the value of aggregated video data for business operations.

brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

paragraphs: EarthDaily is a geospatial company selling satellite imagery and analytics to governments and enterprises whose work depends on the physical world. Its stated purpose is daily monitoring of the earth's surface for broad area change detection.

Raw satellite data is captured through a purpose-built constellation and ground system. That data is then processed, calibrated and quality-controlled into scientifically accurate image products. One product, AiRD, is analysis-ready observation data engineered from the start for machine learning. Its spectral bands are calibrated to match Sentinel-2 and Landsat specifications. A second product, Maritime, is tuned for fast processing and detection of anomalies at sea.

The company focuses its products on agriculture, financial services, infrastructure, forestry and governments. Security organizations, analytics providers and coastal agencies are the named audience for the maritime data. A company timeline states that it was created in partnership with Antarctica Capital. The same timeline lists an acquisition of Descartes Labs and funding from Trinity Capital. It also records more than 500 agreements signed. A news item states the company achieved CEOS Analysis Ready Data compliance.

paragraphs: Alcatraz makes facial authentication products that work with the badge readers and access control systems an organization already runs. The device, called Rock X, sits in line between the badge reader and the access control panel over Wiegand or OSDP.

Employees enroll at a station, remotely from a browser or phone, or automatically after repeated badge swipes at a door fitted with the device. Authentication happens on the device itself, and the company states that no sensitive data is stored or transmitted. Profiles are anonymized and tied to the badge ID already held in the customer's access control system. The same unit can act as a passive second factor, so a person badges in as usual and the face confirms the match. In lobbies it can be built directly into certain turnstiles. The management platform runs on premise or in the cloud.

Airports are one setting the company writes about, pairing face recognition with badges or PINs to add a second factor at restricted doors. One unnamed case summary on the site describes a global enterprise that put the device on turnstiles for more than 150,000 employees. The company says its approach helps customers conform with privacy regulations such as BIPA, CCPA and GDPR.

description: HEXWAVE walk-through concealed weapons detection plus body and shoe scanners for aviation checkpoints and public venues.

paragraphs: Liberty Defense makes AI-based detection equipment for finding concealed weapons and other threats in urban security and aviation settings. Its main product, HEXWAVE, is a walkthrough portal that screens for nonmetallic and metallic threats without asking people to remove shoes, jewelry, belts or jackets.

It uses active millimeter wave, video-rate 3D imaging and AI to detect concealed metallic and non-metallic weapons and other prohibited items. The company says the imaging captures over 400,000 voxels. No images are stored, and none are accessible by the security operator. The operator sees only a go or no-go screen with a clear alert. For aviation, Liberty holds exclusive licenses to two solutions developed by PNNL and funded by the Department of Homeland Security.

The home page states that Liberty delivers HEXWAVE to the TSA. It also says the company is developing screening for aviation workers. Named settings include hotels, schools, airports, public transit systems, places of religion and entertainment venues. On its finances, the company reports completing an initial public offering in the United States that raised approximately $20 million in gross proceeds.

description: LiDAR-based spatial intelligence software turning 3D sensor data into anonymous passenger flow, queue wait time and occupancy analytics for terminals and curbside.

paragraphs: Outsight sells software that turns 3D sensor feeds into a running account of how people, vehicles, and robots move through a site. The buyers are operators of large shared spaces such as airports, hospitals, and factories.

Anything entering the scene is given an anonymous identifier and held to centimeter precision until it leaves. No faces or plates are captured, only the geometry of motion. Operators define zones and the measures they care about, such as counting, density, queue length, wait time and throughput, and the analytics engine computes them continuously. Results come back as live 3D playback, custom indicators, alerts, dashboards, and APIs. Before any of that, a multi-vendor simulator tests layouts and sensor mixes and proposes the hardware configuration.

The company says the platform is deployed at scale across five continents. It calls the result a Motional Digital Twin and says these are running in production. Its newsroom announces a strategic partnership with AWS around spatial AI in aviation. The pitch behind all of it is that movement is the next layer of business to be digitized.

paragraphs: CivicEye sells cloud software for law enforcement and prosecutors, pitched as a way to improve daily workflows and community outcomes. The platform has three main products: a records management system for police called CivicRMS, prosecutor case management called CivicCase, and judicial document management called CivicDocs. A fourth, CivicCase for Courts, is aimed at judges and clerks in municipal courts.

CivicRMS creates NIBRS-compliant reports from incident reports, and its validation tools track errors and point to fixes. Integrations with dispatch and jail systems let officers pull dispatch calls, incident details, arrest records and inmate data without leaving the RMS. CivicDocs holds digital evidence and generates audit logs that track the chain of custody between the arresting agency and the prosecutor's office. Users reach the system through role-based portals for prosecutors, clerks, law enforcement and defense attorneys.

The company traces its start to 2007, when it built software for police departments in upstate New York under the name J2 Software and later Agisent Technologies. It is now based in Charlotte, North Carolina, and says it has deployed its software to over 95 public safety and criminal justice agencies across the country. It also says its prosecutor software is used across Tennessee, where the entire Tennessee District Attorney General's Conference adopted it.

paragraphs: BriefCam sells video analytics software that makes recorded surveillance video searchable, actionable and quantifiable. Its patented VIDEO SYNOPSIS technology condenses hours of surveillance into a short summary by overlaying multiple events, each tagged with its original timestamp, onto a single frame that users can filter by object type and attributes. The software is camera-agnostic, integrates with video management systems such as XProtect, and also works as a standalone solution for agencies that only need file-based review.

Three modules, Review, Respond and Research, are used respectively for post-incident search, real-time alerts and quantifying data trends. Every customer needs Review as a base and can then add Respond, Research or both. License plate recognition works on any camera, with no need for dedicated LPR licenses per camera. For commercial users, people counting tracks queues and crowd movement and measures occupancy to improve space use and traffic flow.

BriefCam serves law enforcement, transportation, retail and more, across public and private sectors. Customer stories on the site cover Tlaxcala, Mexico, Villa El Salvador and the City of Hartford's real-time crime center. The site is published by Milestone Systems, which lists BriefCam among its products alongside the XProtect video management software.

paragraphs: Babel Street sells risk intelligence software to national defense and law enforcement agencies, global enterprises and FinTech companies. Its platform combines rights-cleared global data, governed AI agents and Insights Investigator, its investigation interface. Through that interface analysts submit queries in natural language and receive entity relationships, hidden ownership flags, foreign influence signals and cited evidence. The data behind it spans more than 200 languages, with AI trained to catch slang and coded language that translation alone misses.

For law enforcement, the company says the platform helps agencies investigate and prevent increasingly complex criminal activity. Analysts and police use it to detect early warning signs and uncover behavioral patterns in public data. The identity products process millions of names against watchlists, with matching behavior tuned to reduce false positives and negatives. Border security agencies use the same tools to flag high-risk travelers, cargo and networks.

Its vendor risk product is delivered as secure SaaS or API and embeds continuous monitoring into procurement workflows. Babel Street says a large majority of U.S. national security agencies use it. paragraphs: Miller Mendel, Inc. creates, sells and supports software for city, county, state and federal public safety agencies. Its first and flagship product, eSOPH, is a cloud-based system for public agencies that must run in-depth pre-employment background investigations on their applicants. Since 2011 its customers have been city police departments, county sheriff's offices, state police agencies, district attorney's offices and other criminal justice entities.

The company says eSOPH has been credited with cutting the time to process a background investigation by more than 50%, so applicants can be hired more quickly. Partnerships with Experian and Fama Technologies add one-click retrieval of credit reports and of social media and online activity reports. A captain at the Riverside County Sheriff's Department in California, which conducts over 2,500 applicant investigations a year, estimates a 50% time saving per investigation.

Miller Mendel describes itself as a minority owned, small business. It reports serving over 16,000 agency users. More than 90% of new clients, it says, come by referral from existing eSOPH users. paragraphs: CalAmp sells telematics devices and cloud software that organizations use to monitor, track, and protect vehicles, equipment, and cargo. name: CivicSmart
description: Smart parking meters and occupancy analytics for municipalities

paragraphs: CivicSmart sells cities a curb management system spanning smart hardware at the space, real-time intelligence on every event, enforcement, and the operations software that ties them together. It also aims at universities and campuses. Airports and transit hubs are another target, where rideshare zones, cell lots and passenger loading need managing.

Product lines run from single-space and multi-space meters with integrated sensor options. Curb sensors report real-time occupancy, plate capture, and evidence-grade detection. LaneMaster devices provide automated lane management for loading, pickup-dropoff, rideshare and commercial corridors. Officers write citations on AutoISSUE handhelds. PEMS unifies every meter, sensor, handheld and citation into one dashboard. It publishes open REST endpoints so cities can bring their own BI, GIS and analytics tools.

CivicSmart, Inc. describes itself as a Wisconsin company founded in 2015 around the idea of reimagining the curb. It says it acquired Duncan Parking Technologies from Duncan Solutions in 2015 and renamed it CivicSmart Parking Technologies. The site claims more than 1,500 cities and agencies served. It also claims more than 15 million parking meters shipped. The company says its team holds patents globally for vehicle-detection sensors and parking technologies.

name: PayByPhone
description: Mobile parking payments for city and municipal parking operators

paragraphs: PayByPhone sells a mobile app for paying for parking in a few taps, without coins or hunting for the machine. It is available in over 1,200 cities across North America and Europe, including universities and colleges.

A driver connects a credit or debit card to a PayByPhone account and pays from the phone. Where available, Google Pay or Apple Pay can complete the transaction instead. A session can be extended from the app, with no need to run back to the car to feed the meter.

The company dates its start to 2001 and a plan to take the pain out of parking. It now describes a mission spanning three continents. The home page puts all-time users at more than 125 million. Ownership sits with Lightyear Capital, a New York-based private equity firm with over US$8 billion in assets under management. The press page also announces a global partnership with SKIDATA covering parking and access control solutions. Jonny Combe is named as President and Chief Executive Officer.

paragraphs: Hapco designs, engineers, and manufactures light poles and the hardware that hangs on them, selling to the lighting professionals who specify poles for a project. Its poles show up in street, area, roadway, utility, municipal, and pedestrian lighting work.

The catalog runs from anchor base and direct buried poles to decorative, hinged, solar, camera, and small cell 5G antenna poles. Alongside the poles it sells banner arms in standard and breakaway designs for single and double sided applications. A modular decorative arm system lets a specifier mix interchangeable components into different configurations for a streetscape.

Manufacturing happens in Abingdon, Virginia. The company says its products meet the criteria of the Build America Buy America Act, which matters on publicly funded work. It holds ISO9001:2015 and AISC certifications, and its news page announces Tom Hardy as President and CEO.

description: Workflow automation, online forms and eSignature for state/local agencies - exhibited at Healthcare IT Connect 2026

paragraphs: SimpliGov sells a workflow platform for government agencies, built around the applications, approvals and casework that programs run on. Its stated scope is anything that moves through approvals, whatever the department.

Intake starts with online forms that meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards. Program teams lay out the steps on a drag-and-drop stage builder instead of writing custom code. The engine routes applications and decisions by rule, data threshold and the agency organizational structure. Approvals are signed inside the workflow with native e-signature tools. Dashboards track processing times, bottlenecks and audit trails.

Agency examples include New Castle County processing $322.8 million in emergency grants and passing its audit with zero findings. Another describes a California city automating more than 70 workflows and saving 17,000 labor hours a month. The forms page cites a federal accessibility mandate, 28 CFR Part 35, that larger public entities must meet by April 26, 2027. The platform is described as cloud-native and meeting government data privacy, security and accessibility mandates.

quote.text: SimpliGov executes complex workflows across state and local governments.

paragraphs: PowerTime is scheduling and workforce management software built for public safety agencies. The software covers employee schedules, overtime, leave requests, and time tracking from one secure cloud platform. The stated audience is law enforcement agencies, corrections, fire departments, EMS organizations, emergency communications centers, and other public safety employers.

Overtime lists are built from agency rules, union agreements, FLSA requirements, employee availability, consecutive hours worked, and seniority. Supervisors review employee time, leave requests, overtime, and exceptions from a centralized dashboard. Employees view schedules, request time off, swap shifts, clock in and out, and sign up for available overtime using the web or mobile app. Schedule building covers recurring patrol rotations, fire schedules, dispatcher shifts, and correctional staffing plans under configurable scheduling rules.
