paragraphs: VotingWorks is a nonpartisan nonprofit that builds election technology for the officials who run American elections. There are two products. VxSuite is a complete voting system designed to the latest federal standard. The organization calls it the only open-source voting system used in United States elections. Arlo is an open-source application for auditing vote tabulation after an election.

Voters mark a paper ballot by hand or with a ballot-marking device, then scan it in under three seconds. A full precinct sets up in under three minutes and the equipment folds down for transport. Arlo audits tabulation whether the ballots were counted on VxSuite or on another vendor's system, using peer-reviewed statistics. Source code and documentation are published for anyone to verify. Software integrity can be checked in the field in 30 seconds.

Jurisdictions in New Hampshire and Mississippi run real elections on the voting system. Nine states are listed as using Arlo for statewide risk-limiting audits, among them Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Texas. The work dates to 2018. It is organized as a 501c3, funded by equipment sales and support, government contracts and grants, and donations. The equipment complies with the Help America Vote Act, and HAVA grants can be used to buy it.

paragraphs: Democracy Works is a nonpartisan nonprofit that builds tools meant to make it easier for voters to take part in every election. It works with election officials, major platforms, civic organizations and companies so that voters can reach accurate information.

TurboVote, the voter engagement platform, offers personalized support across the whole voting journey. Underneath it sits official election information collected, verified and published straight from state and local election offices. An Elections API delivers that enterprise-grade data across thousands of elections at every level of government. The Voting Information Project gathers voting location data directly from election officials and distributes it to voters through the Google Civic Information API. Participating jurisdictions are not charged for that program. In 2025 the organization published data for 3,462 elections across all 50 states, covering municipal, school board, county and other local contests.

The organization was founded in 2010 with the goal of making voting easier for Americans. It is a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It has also partnered with platforms such as Perplexity AI and Anthropic to place reliable election information in the AI space. On the employer side, the Civic Alliance it co-founded with the CAA Foundation supports more than 1,300 member businesses.

paragraphs: The business sells a traffic signal priority control platform, marketed as Opticom, to cities that want essential vehicles moving through intersections without delay. It covers two jobs: preemption that clears a path for fire, police and ambulance crews, and signal priority that keeps buses and light rail closer to schedule.

Whichever communication method a city uses, the steps are the same. When a crew activates lights and siren, equipment on the vehicle sends a request ahead to equipped intersections, which then sequence the lights to green on the approach being used. As soon as the vehicle is through, the intersection goes back to its normal cycle. Agencies can run cloud, satellite positioning and infrared deployments side by side rather than replacing everything at once.

The buyers are the people who run those services: fire and police leadership, ambulance directors, transit operations staff and fleet managers. The site dates the technology back close to six decades. Fleets can be connected through integrations with a number of vehicle and telematics vendors.

paragraphs: Ecopia AI uses artificial intelligence to convert high-resolution geospatial imagery into accurate, up-to-date vector maps for data-driven decision-making. For municipal and state government the data is offered for transportation networks, public safety and stormwater planning. Off-the-shelf offerings sit alongside customized global feature extraction.

Its 3D Land Cover product delivers planimetric vector layers for buildings, roads, driveways, sidewalks, water bodies, sports fields and overlapping tree canopy, with height attribution for buildings. The company states that features are extracted from high-resolution imagery with greater than 95% geometric accuracy. Partner imagery providers capture fresh imagery every year, which lets the company detect change and deliver annual updates. A separate transportation product covers sidewalks, crosswalks, medians, bike lanes, turning lanes, paint striping and intersections. Those layers carry attributes such as width, material and feature type, distinguishing a left turn lane from a right turn lane.

The transportation data is aimed at AEC firms, MPOs and DOTs. Stated uses include assessing sidewalk width and curb characteristics against ADA regulations. Another stated use is emergency services and dispatch planning, drawing on 3D maps of buildings, roads and driveways. Ecopia says it produces millions of square kilometers of vector data per month. It also announced a self-serve platform for high-precision geospatial data downloads.

paragraphs: HAAS Alert sells a collision prevention service that sends real-time digital alerts warning drivers about nearby emergency vehicles and roadway hazards. Its customers are fleets that work at the roadside, including tow trucks, utility vehicles, waste management trucks, school buses and snowplows.

The system is wired to a vehicle's warning light bar or master switch, so alerting begins when crews turn on their lights and stops when they turn them off. Motorists install nothing, because alerts are broadcast directly to the navigation platforms they already use. Fleets can activate the service through three primary methods, depending on their existing setup. The company says drivers get up to 30 seconds of advance warning to slow down and move over.

The company traces its start to 2015, when co-founder and CEO Cory Hohs was almost struck by an ambulance on the road. He co-founded the business with Noah Levens and Jigar Patel. Its timeline notes that the United States Department of Homeland Security awarded $1.1 million toward development for digital alerting. It also states that digital alerting was codified and funded in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

A second product works on live feeds rather than uploads, analysing camera streams on the fly and passing traffic data to third-party systems such as traffic management systems and controllers. The company describes the same monitoring applied to bridges and tunnels, where the goal is to prevent congestion and catch accidents early. Alongside direct sales, GoodVision runs a partner program and says it is seeking global distribution and service partners.

paragraphs: Baron Weather sells weather data, forecasting and alerting tools to businesses, government agencies and communities. paragraphs: Dedrone by Axon sells counter-drone systems that secure fixed locations such as airports, correctional facilities and critical infrastructure from unauthorized drones. Law enforcement, military and public safety organizations are named as the buyers for its mobile unit.

A fixed installation combines radio-frequency sensors, radar and pan-tilt-zoom cameras over the airspace at a site. paragraphs: Hidden Level sells radio-frequency sensing hardware and data services to government, defense and commercial security teams. The sensing is passive, which the company says leaves the equipment undetected and hard to jam.

The Breaker sensor is built for fixed sites and is meant to coexist with infrastructure and telecom equipment already there. The Surge mounts to land and water vehicles and is made to withstand harsh conditions. Customers who would rather not run hardware can buy data from a global sensor network the company owns, operates and maintains. Data reaches other systems through an open API secured with FIPS 140-2 compliant cryptography, or through a web interface.

Stated uses include protecting airspace around stadiums, airports and buildings, and preventing contraband drone deliveries to correctional facilities. paragraphs: UVeye builds automated inspection systems that scan the full exterior, undercarriage, and tires of a vehicle in seconds. Dealerships use the scans to document pre-existing damage and avoid unnecessary claims. Seaports and logistics hubs use touchless inspections to speed vehicle handoffs and settle disputes. Bus and truck operators run standardized inspections to improve compliance.

A scan combines high-resolution imaging, sensors, and patented AI to surface problems the eye cannot catch. Findings run from tire wear and misalignment to leaks, rust, and underbody damage. Systems are now deployed across hundreds of dealerships, fleets, rental agencies, and manufacturing lines worldwide. The company names Amazon, General Motors, Volvo, and CarMax among the companies using it. It reports over $380 million raised.

Material runs from basic literacy and GED preparation to college courses and high-demand vocational training. The organization operates exclusively in the corrections space. name: Electro Scan
description: Machine-based pipe defect and leak assessment for municipal sewer and water - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: Electro Scan sells leak detection and lead pipe location work for water and sewer systems. The company says municipal sewer utilities and sewer contractors use it to pin down the location, measurement and flow of defects inside a pipe before a repair or replacement job.

The method rests on a simple claim: pipe defects that leak water also leak electricity, so a defect shows up whether or not it happens to be leaking during the inspection. A low voltage conductivity probe travels through the pipe at 45 to 60 feet per minute, locating and measuring defects as it goes. Crews can then create summary and detail level reports for a team to review. The flagship probe is built for gravity mains between 6 and 30 inches in diameter, and the company says agencies and contractors use it worldwide.

Electro Scan lists ISO 9001:2015 certification for quality management systems. Its case studies page includes a North American benchmark study comparing closed-circuit television inspection with focused electrode leak location on gravity sewer mains. Other write-ups describe a Florida utility dealing with excessive inflow and infiltration in its gravity collection system.

paragraphs: BlueConduit sells predictive modeling tools to water systems that need to manage risk and make data-driven decisions about their distribution assets. The customers are municipalities and water utilities.

One product builds community-specific models that pinpoint high-risk lead and galvanized service lines, which lets a utility classify its inventory and prioritize replacements. Another scores every main segment in a network for likelihood and consequence of failure. A third uses statistical models to confirm the absence of lead in a water system. The company says model processes, important features, and performance metrics are always shared with customers. Output is integrated with Esri ArcGIS.

The work started at the University of Michigan, where faculty and student researchers saw a use for data science in removing toxic lead from the water supply. In Flint the company used predictive analytics to identify where to dig for lead service lines. A published case study describes Des Moines Water Works classifying unknown service lines and reducing uncertainty by 75% in six months. BlueConduit cites ongoing relationships with EPA and state regulators. Its stated mission is to empower communities to prioritize health and sustainability through data science.

paragraphs: 2NDNATURE sells stormwater software built on GIS, aimed at streamlining compliance, asset tracking and reporting. Buyers fall into two camps, those tackling MS4 permit requirements and those advancing corporate water stewardship. Two products carry that work, 2NFORM and Rainsteward, both pitched at streamlining compliance and showing measurable results.

2NFORM is organized around municipal permit programs, covering post-construction, industrial and commercial, and illicit discharge detection and elimination. In Oceanside it was connected to the city's existing Esri-based GIS and met local security and IT standards. For longer-range planning the company built a Stormwater Asset Management Model that serves as a decision-making tool. Fed with the storm sewer system and local costs, it lets a city explore how twenty years of asset management would affect the health of that system. Rainsteward points the other way, at owners trying to cut costs and get more value out of stormwater investments.

The customers shown are city stormwater programs; Oceanside had nine separate systems tracking inspections and compliance tasks before it changed course. Salinas is described as a Phase I MS4 with a population exceeding 150,000. That city worked with 2NDNATURE to develop a comprehensive Asset Improvement Plan. Private owners appear too: a real estate company called Reveler implemented Rainsteward in a series of six steps.

name: Camus Energy
description: Grid orchestration and DER management for municipal utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Camus Energy sells software that electric utilities use to interconnect data centers and local generation. What it sells is the flexible grid connection, in which the utility guarantees firm capacity for most of a site's demand and applies conditional limits to the rest.

Camus uses real utility data to map how much additional load each conductor and substation can safely serve in every hour of the year. Utilities then decide what portion of the load is served firmly and set operating limits for the conditional portion. Day-ahead operating forecasts show when those conditional limits will apply, alongside closed loop controls. The platform pulls SCADA data, GIS assets, network models, AMI, and DER telemetry into one consistent system model. Two applications sit on it: FlexConnect for interconnections and ODMS, which gives utilities a unified view of the distribution grid.

The company says it supports investor-owned and public power utilities. It counts 12 or more utility partners across the United States. It states that joint studies with Google, AES, and Princeton's ZERO Lab set the benchmark for how utilities and developers evaluate flexibility and grid capacity. On security, it says OAuth authentication, MFA, role-based access, audit logging, and continuous monitoring protect the platform.

paragraphs: Neara sells physics-based digital twin software to electric utilities, which use it to model their networks. The pitch is to unify assets, surroundings and workflows in a single physics-accurate view.

Wildfire work pulls pole loading, asset condition, vegetation, GIS accuracy, weather and consequence into one physics-backed model. Resiliency work prioritizes mitigation by how asset condition, vegetation proximity and environmental conditions interact across the network. paragraphs: Copperleaf sells decision analytics software that helps large organizations decide how to spend limited money on the infrastructure they own. The buyers are agencies and companies running critical infrastructure, where choices about maintenance, sustainment, or growth projects always involve a trade-off. The site groups the work by industry, among them electric utilities, government, rail and transit, roads and highways, and water and wastewater.

The method puts every proposed investment on a common footing so dissimilar options can be compared objectively. A single collaborative repository stores all asset and investment data, with proposals entered in one format and common financial metrics. Analytics then weigh hundreds of thousands of possible investments and return an optimal plan, with what-if scenarios for different budgets, timing, and constraints. A companion product, Copperleaf Asset, forecasts the long-term risk exposure of an entire asset population and bundles planned interventions to reduce service outages.

The company says its decision analytics is used to manage over $2.9 trillion of assets globally. Copperleaf is now paired with IFS, aimed at asset-intensive organizations allocating capital and operating expenditure. Its planning approach is described as embodying the key principles of ISO 55000. The enterprise software also connects to existing EAM, APM, ERP, and GIS systems.

The same alcohol system is used in nine other states and two provinces for alcohol industry regulation. name: Symbium

paragraphs: Symbium runs an instant permitting service that lets homeowners and contractors see what a property allows, scope a project such as solar panels or a heat pump, and then file and manage the permit application. Compliance checks run against the applicable building, zoning, and energy codes while the applicant is still scoping the work. The technology underneath, called Complaw, is described as a TurboTax-like mechanization of regulatory analysis first built by the founding team at Stanford AI Lab. It layers onto the permitting workflows a building department already has, with contractors getting issuance within seconds of applying.

Contractors use it to accelerate permit issuance across a range of project types. The company says it has saved contractors and city staff time, and puts the running total at 3,500,000 project hours so far. It names Elemental Impact, Third Derivative, Uptake Alliance, and IMPEL among its backers. It was founded by Leila Banijamali, Abhijeet Mohapatra and Michael Genesereth during work at Stanford University. Recognition it lists includes a California Building Officials industry achievement award and a United States Conference of Mayors Civic Challenge.

The company says a city's code text can be digitized in as little as four weeks.

The company says Archistar was founded by Dr. Benjamin Coorey in 2010 and began life as an education portal. It grew from a university research project into a platform that could read planning rules, run feasibility tests and generate compliant designs in minutes. The site states that Archistar powers digital planning for over 30 cities and governments across Australia, Canada and the United States. Among the municipalities it names supporting are LA County, the City of Los Angeles, the City of Austin and the City of New York. Offices are listed across Los Angeles, Vancouver and Sydney.

paragraphs: Civica makes software that public bodies use to deliver critical services to citizens around the world. It says over 6,000 public bodies use that software to help provide critical services to over 100 million citizens.

Its solutions span local and central government, health and community care, housing and social care, libraries and education, and regulatory and compliance services. The company describes integrated cloud platforms that automate workflows, support data-driven decision-making and reduce operational costs. Named products include Spydus, a library management system. Civica also sells master data management for state and local government. It says it is an approved supplier on major government frameworks.

Civica was established in 2001 and describes itself as one of the UK's largest software companies. Its team has grown to 5,500 colleagues, one-third of whom have worked in the sectors it serves. Acquisitions are part of the strategy, with more than 37 completed in the last 10 years. The company reports delivery in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, India, North America and Europe. Customer stories on its site include delivering a single citizen view for the State of Alaska.

name: Ecolane
description: Paratransit and microtransit scheduling software for public transit agencies

paragraphs: Ecolane sells scheduling and dispatch software designed for public transit agencies that operate paratransit, non-emergency medical transportation, and microtransit services. Whichever way a trip is booked, the optimization that follows is autonomous and does not require manual intervention from a human.

The software optimizes service at the individual trip level and updates schedules as conditions change during the service day. That lets agencies account for no-shows, cancellations, delays, and staffing changes without rebuilding schedules manually. Eligibility rules, reporting, and compliance are integrated into daily operations. Managers can capture data for every vehicle, including rides per hour, run utilization, on-time performance, and deadhead. For medical trips, the platform helps agencies locate providers, verify rider eligibility, and schedule trips with vehicles equipped to accommodate rider needs.

Agencies supported by city, county, state, or federal funds are the intended buyers. The company says it is a U.S.-based company with U.S.-based product, engineering, and support teams. It states that its self-service applications are compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act and Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 Level AA. It also says it holds three clean Voluntary Product Accessibility Templates. The hosted service is described as providing significant cost savings for transit agencies.

name: Blaise Transit
description: Demand-responsive transit dispatch and booking software for transit agencies - exhibited at CTAA EXPO 2026

paragraphs: Blaise Transit sells software for running transit without a fixed route or a fixed schedule. It was built to equip municipalities, cities, transit agencies, and transit operators. One platform covers demand-responsive service, paratransit, fixed-route integrations, and private shuttles.

The system comes in three parts. Blaise Engine lets operators set the vehicles, drivers, stops, and payment options that make up a transit system. A passenger app is available on Android, iOS, and as a website, where riders book, pay, and follow live vehicle locations. A driver app supplies turn-by-turn navigation on optimized routes and a passenger manifest at each stop. A separate simulations service recommends which transit models to implement and the parameters for each service.

Blaise was started in 2018 by a small group of transit-loving engineers. The site says more than 70 communities have chosen it to optimize their transit services. It reports working with agencies serving a few hundred rides a month up to a few million. Its optimization models are described as patent pending and customizable.

name: EasyMile

paragraphs: EasyMile makes autonomous driving software for vehicles working at airports, logistics sites and industrial sites around the world. The company supplies the autonomous driving intelligence, a CE-marked stack handling perception, path planning and safety. The vehicles it powers are distributed by TractEasy.

One of them is a heavy-duty autonomous tow tractor built for airports, factories and logistics hubs. It is described as running around the clock with a single operator overseeing an entire fleet. The other is a cargo dolly for air cargo and ground handling operations. It carries up to 7 metric tonnes while navigating around personnel and ground equipment. The software is meant to be modular enough to power other kinds of heavy-duty vehicles as well.

EasyMile says it was founded in 2014 between Singapore and Toulouse. Its timeline starts with a first passenger fleet on the road in Lausanne, Switzerland. The same timeline names Alstom, Bpifrance and Continental as investors backing the company. It records driving in autonomous mode in more than 300 locations worldwide. The company also claims to be the first autonomous technology provider to obtain ISO 9001:2015 certification.

What it sells is more than the vehicle: the offer covers integration of the vehicles into a given environment and fleet management alongside them. Testing of the earlier Iseauto shuttle on Estonian public streets began in the summer of 2020. One case study describes a scheduled last mile service in Takamatsu, Japan, with the shuttle operated by Boldly. That route ran 2.6 kilometres between a car park and a viewpoint.

paragraphs: CP Group designs, manufactures, installs, and services sorting machinery for the waste and recycling industry. It sells turnkey systems for both new material recovery facilities and retrofits of existing ones. A project management team handles third parties, scheduling, shipping, and installation.

Designing a facility begins with collaborative design meetings, cost reviews, and civil and electrical considerations. The equipment itself is engineered and manufactured in the United States. The shop has 115,000 sq. ft. of manufacturing space and 435,600 sq. ft. of storage on 9 acres. At startup and commissioning, the team goes over compliance, operations, and safety with the customer. Support afterward covers spare parts, process upgrades, and troubleshooting.

The company dates its machinery to the invention of the first commercial aluminum can flattener in 1977, and its name to Can Pac. It later acquired Krause Manufacturing, which makes construction and demolition separation equipment, and Advanced MRF, a specialist in intelligent motor controls and data acquisition. It says it owned and operated a material recovery facility for over 25 years, processing half of the city of San Diego's curbside recycling. That adds up to nearly 50 years of hands-on experience by its own account.

Video and telematics data upload to the cloud, where they become safety events that a review team turns into driver coaching material. A maintenance module watches the chassis, body and equipment continuously. It hands mechanics a list of repairs ranked by severity or by how long remains before failure. The company presents itself as part of Environmental Solutions Group alongside Soft-Pak and Heil, under the Connected Collections banner. paragraphs: Balancing Act sells simulation-based public engagement tools to government. The company describes an online simulation that draws stakeholders in so that leaders can make hard choices with public input behind them. The suite is aimed at budget, housing, climate and planning work.

In a budget simulation, residents see a model of the budget and their input is collected. A companion tool asks a few questions, estimates the taxes a household pays and shows where those dollars go. A mode for meetings turns the simulation into a facilitation tool for in-person and online sessions. There is also a research version for use with representative samples. The Prioritize product goes past a survey by having users pick items and then rank their picks. Its consensus analysis reports how many stakeholders end up with at least one of their choices included.

The housing product addresses cities and counties that struggle with public participation as they try to meet demand for new housing. Those simulations put residents in the shoes of decisionmakers and ask them to help solve the problem, with an interactive map showing where housing would be placed. Prioritize has been offered for input on stimulus funds such as ARPA and ESSER. A testimonial on the site is attributed to a village administrator in Germantown, Wisconsin.

Muni-Link says it helps municipal utilities, utility authorities, water districts, and regulated utilities manage their accounts. The software is described as built for cities, towns, and the people who serve them. Unlimited support is built into the subscription fee at no extra cost. description: Municipal bond market data, debt structuring, and issuer debt management software for government finance officers, underwriters, and municipal advisors - exhibited at GFOA 2026

paragraphs: MuniPro sells a workstation for municipal finance built on the record of each issuer's debt, covering every series and maturity, every refunding and defeasance, and obligations that never carried a CUSIP. Fourteen named tools sit on one system of record, and market data is sourced and stamped so results are reproducible.

The workspace groups debt management, debt structuring, refunding scenarios, market data, option pricing and bond holders, each reading from the same record. Debt structuring toggles between level debt, wrap-around and ascending structures and layers reserve funds, capitalized interest and bond insurance. Option pricing runs a Black-Derman-Toy binomial tree for option-adjusted spreads with custom volatility, short-rate and curve assumptions.

Five roles share one workspace: investment bankers, underwriters, credit analysts, municipal advisors and portfolio managers. Each module replaces a single-purpose subscription on a typical desk, and bought together they are described as cheaper than any two of the legacy tools. Government finance officers are pointed to BondGov, a free sister platform for state and local issuers, with no charge for any government in the U.S.

paragraphs: CHESS Health sells digital health software aimed at the substance use disorder crisis, for providers, health plans, and public sector organizations. Its public sector buyers are described as state health and behavioral health departments, county, tribal and local governments, drug courts, and correctional facilities. On the clinical side the site lists SUD providers, detox facilities, hospitals and emergency departments, clinics, FQHCs, and CCBHCs. Payers listed include managed care organizations, Medicaid plans, and commercial insurance.

Connections, the patient-facing app, offers 24/7 access to peer support, meetings, and recovery tools. Patients can be signed up automatically, with every patient invited to the app through EHR integration. A second product, eIntervention, is described as streamlining referrals and access to support services for substance use and mental health. A third, eRecovery, covers patient communication, progress tracking, and 24/7 peer support.

Published case studies include a county coalition in Hancock County, Ohio expanding its reach through community engagement. In one clinic case study, 83% of new patients using the app were still in treatment against 61% of those not using it.

name: CredibleMind
description: Behavioral health and wellbeing content, screening, and care-navigation platform deployed by public health departments, health plans, and health systems for their communities - exhibited at NatCon 2026, NACCHO 360 2026

paragraphs: CredibleMind partners with health plans, health systems, employers, and communities to break down the barriers of stigma, navigation, and cost that keep people from mental health care. Its platform blends evidence-based self-care, early intervention, and screening-based navigation into one integrated experience.

People start with validated assessments, and each customer configures referral rules and custom questions that triage higher-acuity needs to in-network care. The catalog runs to over a dozen assessments and more than 100 content topic centers. Behind those sit more than 10,000 evidence-rated resources that the company describes as grounded in science. The experience is designed for accessibility and available in 38 languages. APIs and EHR integrations tie the platform into clinical workflows.

The company says it works with more than 150 partners and supports over 40 million lives. Its stated partners include public sector agencies and community organizations. Deryk Van Brunt is a co-founder of the company and serves as its chief executive. Marcos Athanasoulis, also a co-founder, serves as chief technology officer.

name: Gimlet
description: Hosted reference desk statistics tracking and reporting software for public and academic libraries - exhibited at PLA 2026

paragraphs: Gimlet is hosted software for keeping track of what happens at a service desk. It is sold to libraries and other organizations that want to see the trends and patterns behind the questions their desks field.

Staff log each interaction on a form the organization configures with its own category values. Entries can be tagged, and the full text of a question and its answer is kept so it can be searched later. A search can cover every entry or narrow to a single building or desk. Reports can show which desks are busiest at which hours of the week and which staff field the hardest questions. Data can be moved out to spreadsheet or reporting tools such as Excel, Google Sheets or Tableau. A web browser is all a desk needs to use it, and there is no cap on the number of staff or computers on an account.

Gimlet was founded by Eric Larson, a librarian, and Nate Vack, a library web application developer. The site puts the running total at more than 106,929,217 questions answered. The service is monitored around the clock for uptime, performance and security, with data mirrored, encrypted and backed up. Customers keep ownership of the data they enter. A 30-day free trial is offered.

paragraphs: FeedbackFruits sells teaching activities that run inside a university's own learning management system, so neither instructors nor students need a second login. The activities pull assessment, collaboration and feedback into a course in a few clicks.

Peer Review carries the whole process from assignment submission through to graded feedback. An instructor decides whether students review each other individually or as teams. It can generate discussion prompts and quiz questions to speed up course design. A newer activity, Oral Practice, has students talk through their reasoning with that AI or with a peer, around work they submitted or a skill. Every session is recorded and stored without extra admin.

The site claims use at more than 200 institutions worldwide. It also counts over 5,000 educators. Testimonials on the peer review page are attributed to staff such as a director of academic technology at a school of public health. An institution can start with a supported pilot before committing further. The company points to recognised security standards and certifications, and offers human support to teachers and students five days a week.

name: Cirrus Identity
description: Managed SAML and CAS identity federation, SSO, and guest-identity services for higher education institutions - exhibited at EDUCAUSE 2026

paragraphs: Cirrus Identity sells hosted sign-on services to colleges and universities of all sizes, university systems, research institutions, and medical centers. The problem it addresses is that campus identity systems were never designed to work together. Instead of replacing what a school already runs, Cirrus proxies authentication across identity providers, federations, and legacy systems.

The Bridge solution provides multilateral SAML and CAS for Entra ID, Okta, Duo SSO, and others. That lets a school meet the multilateral federation requirements of eduGAIN federations such as InCommon, CAF, and GakuNin without running Shibboleth, ADFS, or SSP. The Proxy solution handles people outside the enterprise directory, so guests, collaborators, alumni, and lifelong learners sign in without being given enterprise identities. Those users can bring credentials from Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn, Amazon, Apple, an ORCID iD, or a Cirrus Identity OrgBrandedID. Applicants can sign in to selected applications with their existing Slate credentials.

The buyers named on the site are identity and access management, security and privacy, systems architect, and enterprise application teams. Administrators get a console for reaching log events and configuring the products. The service is fully cloud hosted with 24x365 production support. Pricing is an annual subscription plus a one-time implementation fee, quoted for each use case. The company calls itself an InCommon Catalyst community partner.

The service tailors each resume, searches job boards and company sites, applies on the candidate's behalf, schedules interviews, preps the candidate, and captures the offer letter and verification of employment. paragraphs: LeakZon, established 2023, develops an analytical solution that reduces the water loss rate, also known as Non-Revenue Water. It collects and analyzes raw AMR, GIS maps, CIS and other relevant environmental data. Proprietary AI tools optimize the District Metered Areas and detect water anomalies such as leaks, metering inaccuracies, unauthorized consumption and abnormal usage.

Continuous analysis of meter and SCADA data flags leaks, bursts and night-flow anomalies as soon as they appear. The platform creates virtual DMAs that split a water network into virtual zones without physical works or new sensors. An onboarding wizard gathers data from GIS, meters, SCADA, billing and other sources and builds a digital picture of the network. Once onboarded, the platform monitors the network around the clock and turns each anomaly into a managed issue. The platform follows the AWWA M36 water audit methodology, classifying every drop from system input volume down to revenue and non-revenue water.

The homepage states that LeakZon serves the whole water ecosystem. Utilities are the audience for the alerts, dispatching crews to the locations the AI pinpoints. Water service providers are a second named segment, with LeakZon offered to them as a value-added service. LeakZon already operates across the United States, including Texas, California, Illinois, Pennsylvania and Florida.

name: BiblioCommons
description: Patron-facing catalog discovery, website, mobile app, events calendar and email marketing platform for public library systems - exhibited at PLA 2026

paragraphs: BiblioCommons builds the online side of a public library, covering the catalog, mobile app, website, events calendar and email marketing. The pieces are sold as a suite intended to work as one.

BiblioCore is the discovery layer, presented as more than an online repository of a library's collections. Search uses facets and FRBRised grouping so patrons can find titles the way they search elsewhere on the web. Accessibility features include screen reader support, color contrast compliance, keyboard access, grouped search and text resizing. Reviews and lists contributed by patrons are shared across all BiblioCore libraries. Add-on modules offer interface languages ranging from Filipino, French, Japanese and Korean to Spanish and Vietnamese. Another synchronizes eContent metadata directly from providers so the collection shows in the catalog. BiblioFines integrates with PayPal and the ILS so patrons can settle payments online.

The catalog is vendor agnostic and integrates the products and services public libraries subscribe to. The company says it began as a non-profit youth literacy initiative before turning to library catalogs. Three Canadian provincial agencies funded prototypes and purchased advanced subscriptions in the early years. After a year-long beta with six libraries, the re-architected services were re-launched. Staff are described as coming from both technical and library backgrounds.

paragraphs: Mango Languages sells language courses covering more than 70 languages and dialects, plus English for speakers of more than 20 others. Individuals subscribe, and the company also offers custom arrangements for organizations of any size.

The system follows vaccine inventory from ordering through delivery and administration. Clinic record systems send administered doses straight into the registry, which cuts duplicate entry.
